doctrine:
Under **Section 19 of Executive Order No. 1008** (Construction Industry Arbitration Law), a CIAC arbitral award is **final and unappealable except on questions of law**. Reiterating *Global Medical Center of Laguna, Inc. v. Ross Systems International, Inc.*, the Court held that the CIAC's factual findings may be reviewed only on narrow, **"tribunal-centered" and not "fact-centered"** grounds: (1) a challenge to the integrity of the arbitral tribunal, i.e., (i) the award was procured by corruption, fraud or other undue means; (ii) evident partiality or corruption of the arbitrators; (iii) misconduct in refusing to postpone the hearing upon sufficient cause or in refusing to hear pertinent and material evidence; (iv) an arbitrator disqualified under Section 9 of RA 876 wilfully refrained from disclosing it, or other misbehavior materially prejudiced a party; or (v) the arbitrators exceeded their powers or so imperfectly executed them that no mutual, final and definite award was made; and (2) an allegation that the tribunal violated the Constitution or positive law. **Mere disagreement with the tribunal's appreciation of the evidence, or perceived errors of fact, does not open the award to review.** A party invoking partiality or ground (v) must satisfactorily show that the arbitrators were compromised or that their integrity could not be relied upon.

The reviewing court asks two questions. First, is the issue one of law or of fact? If of law, the award may be appealed. Second, if of fact, is it only a disagreement with the tribunal's factual conclusions (not reviewable), or does it go into the integrity of the tribunal in a manner amounting to grave abuse of discretion (reviewable)? **Whether undisputed and authentic documents legally amount to an agreement to extend the completion date, or to a waiver of the contractual notice requirement for an extension, is a question of law.** Who caused the delay, whether the grounds for termination existed, and how much of the downpayment or rectification cost remains due are questions of fact. (The Court noted that *Global Medical Center*'s ruling on the modes of review, Rule 45 to the Supreme Court on questions of law and Rule 65 to the CA on factual issues involving grave abuse, applies prospectively and did not govern this case, but its exposition of reviewable factual issues applies squarely.)

On the merits: a **waiver must be clear and unequivocal**, and there is no implied waiver without a clear, unequivocal and decisive act. Letting the contractor continue working past the completion date, agreeing to acceleration measures, and extending the performance bond do not waive the contract's extension-of-time procedure, because a contractor's delay does not end the contract; it only makes the contractor liable for delay damages while its duty to finish remains, and an owner who keeps the project going is mitigating damages under **Article 2203 of the Civil Code**. Attorney's fees under **Article 2208** and costs of arbitration cannot be awarded without a finding that the losing party resisted the claim in bad faith (reiterated).
facts:
On June 30, 2014, Roxaco (employer) and Gulf Canary (contractor) signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) for the construction of a 12-storey, 199-room hotel on Quirino Avenue, Parañaque City, for PHP 219,822,703.36. Roxaco paid a 20% downpayment of PHP 45,638,494.74 on September 3, 2014. On September 17, 2014, the parties executed a FIDIC Contract. Gulf Canary posted a Performance Bond of PHP 65,946,811.06 (30% of the price) issued by Asia United on July 4, 2014, which would expire on July 8, 2015. The MOA required completion by March 31, 2015 "unless an extension of time has been authorized and approved by the Employer in writing in accordance with the conditions stated in the FIDIC Contract." FIDIC Sub-Clause 20.1 required the contractor to give notice of a claim for extension within 28 days after it became aware of the event; otherwise "the Time for Completion shall not be extended."

The hotel was not finished by March 31, 2015. The parties agreed to augment Gulf Canary's resources, and Roxaco nominated Vision Properties as subcontractor. A March 16, 2015 letter from Pure Projects (Roxaco's project manager, acting as Engineer) recorded that Roxaco would not terminate Gulf Canary, and that Gulf Canary acknowledged it could not meet the completion date, which "will result in a claim for damages" for delay at 1/10 of 1% of the contract price per day. On July 7, 2015, Roxaco called on the Performance Bond, citing Gulf Canary's breach and its failure to deliver an extended bond, and stating that the extended work completion "would be until January 31, 2016." Asia United did not respond. On September 18, 2015, with only 34.92% of the works done, Roxaco terminated the contracts and engaged Vision to rectify and complete the works. Its demand on Gulf Canary dated September 22, 2017 went unanswered.

Roxaco sued Gulf Canary and Asia United before the CIAC. Gulf Canary claimed the completion date had been extended to January 31, 2016; Asia United claimed it was released because the contract was varied without its consent. The CIAC Tribunal's Final Award of September 24, 2018 found no valid extension, declared the termination valid and the bond subsisting, and ordered Gulf Canary to pay PHP 14,305,098.96 as liquidated damages, PHP 29,701,532.37 as recoupment of the downpayment, rectification costs, 6% interest from September 22, 2017, PHP 2,500,000.00 as attorney's fees, and the costs of arbitration. It denied the claim for cost of completion and held Asia United jointly and severally liable up to the amount of the bond.

On Rule 43 petitions, the CA reversed and dismissed Roxaco's complaint. It held that whether the completion date was extended is a question of law and, alternatively, that the arbitrators "exceeded their powers" by ignoring documents showing an extension. It ruled that the 28-day notice requirement was waived by the parties' acts: the March 13, 2015 meeting minutes on acceleration, the March 16, 2015 letter, Roxaco's July 7, 2015 letter, the extension of the bond to January 31, 2016, and Notices to Correct dated August 24, 2015. So there was no delay, the termination was premature, and the surety was not liable. Roxaco filed a Rule 45 petition.
issues: Whether the issue of whether the completion date was validly extended is a question of law that the CA could review, and whether the parties agreed to an extension or waived the contractual notice requirement.
Whether the CA could review the CIAC Tribunal's factual findings on Gulf Canary's delay and the validity of the termination on the ground that the arbitrators exceeded their powers or were partial.
Whether the CA erred in dismissing Roxaco's claims for recoupment of the downpayment and for rectification costs.
Whether Roxaco is entitled to attorney's fees and costs of arbitration.
Whether Asia United was released from its surety obligation by an alleged variation or novation of the construction contracts.
ruling:
**1. Yes, it is a question of law, but there was no valid extension.** A question of law exists when the issue does not call for an examination of the probative value of the evidence, the truth of the facts being admitted; asking whether the evidence suffices to support a legal conclusion also raises a question of law (*New Rural Bank of Guimba v. Abad*; *Republic v. Vega*). The parties did not dispute that Gulf Canary sent no written notice under Sub-Clause 20.1, nor the existence and authenticity of the documents the CA relied on. The only question was their legal significance. The CA nonetheless drew the wrong conclusion. Under the MOA and Sub-Clause 20.1, Gulf Canary was not entitled to an extension. A waiver must be "clear and unequivocal," and none of the documents showed one. The CA wrongly assumed that Roxaco would have terminated the contract if Gulf Canary were in delay. Missing the completion date did not end the contract: under Sub-Clause 8.7, delay damages "shall not relieve the Contractor from his obligation to complete the Works," and the MOA imposed a daily penalty of 1/10 of 1% for delay. Continuing the works only meant Gulf Canary still had to finish, subject to its liability for delay; the March 16, 2015 letter itself said the delay "will result in a claim for damages." Extending the bond protected Roxaco while the works went on; agreeing to accelerate was consistent with the duty to mitigate under Article 2203; and the July 7, 2015 letter was a call on the bond precisely because of Gulf Canary's breach. The CIAC Tribunal's finding of no valid extension was affirmed.

**2. No, these are questions of fact that could not be reviewed.** Who caused the delay was determined by the CIAC Tribunal after examining the evidence. The CA's reason (the tribunal "gave a cold shoulder" to the documents) and Gulf Canary's charge of partiality were only disagreements with the tribunal's appreciation of the evidence. **"That a party disagrees with the conclusions of an arbitral tribunal will not suffice to charge such a tribunal with partiality and warrant a judicial review of the arbitral award's factual findings."** Allowing such appeals would undermine the speed and expertise that make CIAC arbitration valuable and would relegate the CIAC to "a first level court." The finding that the termination grounds under Sub-Clause 15.2 (failure to comply with a Notice to Correct, abandonment, failure to proceed) were "well-documented" was likewise binding.

**3. Yes, the CA erred.** These claims did not depend on the extension issue. The downpayment was an advance payment, described by the tribunal as an "interest-free loan" repaid through percentage deductions in payment certificates (Sub-Clause 14.2). The unpaid balance of PHP 29,701,532.37 and the existence and cost of defects attributable to Gulf Canary were factual findings with no ground for review. Gulf Canary's liability for rectification costs rested on the MOA (defects corrected at the contractor's cost) and FIDIC Sub-Clauses 4.1, 11.1 and 11.2.

**4. No.** Attorney's fees are not recovered as a rule, because no premium is placed on the right to litigate. An award under Article 2208 "demands factual, legal, and equitable justification"; even a party compelled to litigate may be denied fees where the other side's persistence shows no bad faith beyond "an erroneous conviction of the righteousness of his [or her] cause" (*President of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints v. BTL Construction Corp.*). The tribunal made no finding of bad faith. For the same reason, the award of costs of arbitration was deleted.

**5. No.** Asia United relied on Article 1215 of the Civil Code (novation with a solidary debtor extinguishes the obligation) and the March 16, 2015 letter. But the tribunal found that Pure Projects had no authority to modify the MOA and that Roxaco never agreed to modify it, so no variation or novation was made. That factual finding was binding. **Asia United is solidarily liable with Gulf Canary up to the amount of the Performance Bond.**
disposition: Petition GRANTED. The CA Decision of March 27, 2019 in CA-G.R. SP Nos. 157863 and 157866 was REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The CIAC Final Award of September 24, 2018 in CIAC Case No. 45-2017 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION: Roxaco is not entitled to attorney's fees and costs of arbitration. The monetary award earns legal interest of 6% per annum from finality of the Decision until fully paid.

bar_questions.q: BuildCo and Hotel Corp. arbitrated a construction dispute before the CIAC. After hearing both sides, the Arbitral Tribunal found that BuildCo caused the delay in the project and awarded Hotel Corp. liquidated damages. BuildCo seeks judicial review, arguing that the Tribunal gave too much weight to Hotel Corp.'s witnesses and "ignored" BuildCo's site reports, which shows that the arbitrators exceeded their powers and were partial to Hotel Corp. BuildCo offers no other proof of partiality. May the reviewing court re-examine and reverse the Tribunal's finding on who caused the delay?

alac.answer: No. The finding on who caused the delay is a factual finding that is final and not subject to review.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 19 of Executive Order No. 1008, a CIAC arbitral award is final and unappealable except on questions of law. Factual findings may be reviewed only on tribunal-centered grounds: a challenge to the integrity of the tribunal (corruption, fraud or undue means; evident partiality; misconduct in refusing to postpone or to hear material evidence; undisclosed disqualification; or the arbitrators exceeding their powers so that no mutual, final and definite award was made), or a violation of the Constitution or positive law. Mere disagreement with the tribunal's appreciation of the evidence does not suffice, and a party claiming partiality must satisfactorily show that the arbitrators were compromised. (Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc., G.R. Nos. 246250-51, September 29, 2025, reiterating Global Medical Center of Laguna, Inc. v. Ross Systems International, Inc.)
alac.application: Who caused the delay requires weighing the evidence, so it is a question of fact. BuildCo's complaint is that the Tribunal believed Hotel Corp.'s witnesses over its own site reports. That is a disagreement with the Tribunal's appreciation of the evidence, not proof that the arbitrators were corrupt, partial or otherwise compromised. Calling it "exceeding their powers" does not change its nature. Allowing such a challenge would turn the CIAC into a first-level court and defeat the speed and expertise that justify construction arbitration.
alac.conclusion: The reviewing court may not re-examine or reverse the Tribunal's finding that BuildCo caused the delay.

bar_questions.q: Under a construction contract, the completion date was June 30, 2025, and the contractor could get an extension only by giving the owner written notice of its claim within 28 days from the event causing delay; otherwise "the time for completion shall not be extended." The contractor never gave such notice. After June 30, 2025, the owner let the contractor keep working, agreed to measures to speed up the works, and required the contractor to extend its performance bond to March 31, 2026. The owner later terminated the contract and claimed delay damages. The contractor argues that the owner's acts waived the notice requirement and extended the completion date. The authenticity of all the documents is admitted. (a) Is the issue a question of law or of fact? (b) Did the owner waive the notice requirement and extend the completion date?

alac.answer: (a) It is a question of law. (b) No. The owner's acts do not amount to a waiver or an extension.
alac.legal_basis: A question of law exists when the issue does not call for an examination of the probative value of the evidence, the facts being admitted, and the only question is the legal significance of the evidence. A waiver must be clear and unequivocal, and there is no implied waiver without a clear, unequivocal and decisive act showing that purpose. A contractor's failure to meet the completion date does not end the contract; it only makes the contractor liable for delay damages while its obligation to finish remains. An owner who keeps the project going is mitigating its damages under Article 2203 of the Civil Code. (Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc., G.R. Nos. 246250-51, September 29, 2025)
alac.application: (a) Since no one disputes that no notice was given or that the documents are genuine, the court need not weigh credibility. It only has to decide what these admitted acts mean in law, which is a question of law. (b) Allowing the contractor to continue simply meant the contractor still had to finish the works, subject to delay damages. Agreeing to accelerate the works was the owner's effort to minimize its loss. Requiring a longer performance bond protected the owner while the works continued. None of these acts clearly and unequivocally shows an intent to give up the 28-day notice requirement or to move the completion date.
alac.conclusion: The question is one of law, and the completion date was not extended, so the contractor was in delay after June 30, 2025.

bar_questions.q: In the same CIAC case, the Arbitral Tribunal (a) awarded the owner attorney's fees solely because the owner "was compelled to obtain the services of counsel to protect its interest," with no finding of bad faith on the contractor's part; and (b) held the surety solidarily liable on the performance bond up to its face amount. The surety argues that it was released because a letter from the owner's project manager modified the contract without the surety's consent. The Tribunal had found that the project manager had no authority to modify the contract and that the owner never agreed to any modification. Rule on (a) and (b).

alac.answer: (a) The award of attorney's fees is improper. (b) The surety is not released and remains solidarily liable up to the amount of the bond.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, attorney's fees are not recoverable as a rule, since no premium is placed on the right to litigate; an award demands factual, legal and equitable justification, and is not proper where the losing party's resistance reflects no bad faith beyond an erroneous belief in the righteousness of its cause. Under Article 1215 of the Civil Code, novation with a solidary debtor extinguishes the obligation, but whether a novation or variation happened is a question of fact, and the CIAC's factual findings are binding absent a tribunal-centered ground for review. (Roxaco-Asia Hospitality Corp. v. Gulf Canary Construction and Development, Inc., G.R. Nos. 246250-51, September 29, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The only basis for the fees was that the owner had to hire counsel. The Tribunal made no finding that the contractor resisted the claim in bad faith or refused to pay without justifiable cause. Losing on the merits is not bad faith, so the fees (and, for the same reason, an award of costs of arbitration) should be deleted. (b) The surety's defense depends on a modification of the contract, but the Tribunal found as a fact that the project manager had no authority to modify it and that the owner did not agree to any change. With no showing that the Tribunal's integrity was compromised, that finding stands, and there was no novation to release the surety.
alac.conclusion: The attorney's fees must be deleted, but the surety stays solidarily liable with the contractor up to the amount of the performance bond.

notes: The rectification cost is PHP 16,964,878.38 in the CIAC fallo as quoted, but PHP 16,964,858.38 in the Court's discussion; the Court affirmed the amount determined by the CIAC Tribunal. The CIAC fallo as quoted makes Asia United liable "in respect of items (i) and (vi)" up to the bond amount. The Court introduced the rule on costs of arbitration as "Section 15 of the CIAC Revised Rules of Procedure" but quoted "SECTION 16.5." One co-arbitrator (Atty. Julius A. Omilia) dissented from the Final Award. The case reached the CA by Rule 43 petitions; under Global Medical Center (applied prospectively), questions of law go to the Supreme Court under Rule 45 and factual issues involving grave abuse go to the CA under Rule 65.
